subject: science

items.q: In science, what is a pure substance?
items.correct: Just one substance, with nothing mixed in
items.misconception: A natural material with nothing added to it
items.why: Adverts and labels use 'pure' to mean natural or with nothing added ('pure orange juice', 'pure spring water'). Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on introducing chemical reactions, reports Johnson (1996): 11–14-year-olds 'think of rock salt as "pure" but extracted salt as "impure" because it has gone through a chemical process'; the RSC Education resource 'What do chemical words mean?' lists 'A pure substance is something that occurs in nature' as a misconception. Ask what is in the material, not where it came from. If it contains only one substance it is pure; if it contains two or more, it is a mixture, even if it is natural.
items.specStatementText: the concept of a pure substance
items.random_wrong: A material that looks clear and clean

items.q: A label says 'Pure spring water: natural, with nothing added'. Spring water has minerals dissolved in it. What is it to a scientist?
items.correct: A mixture of water and minerals
items.misconception: A pure substance, as it looks so clear
items.why: Students judge materials by what they can see, and the composition of a material is not visible. That this leads them to call clear solutions or one-colour inks pure is our inference from the finding that follows. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) notes that students 'are more likely to focus upon a material's appearance and its common uses' than on its composition. Purity is about what is in the material, and you often cannot see it. Test it instead: a pure substance has a sharp melting or boiling point and gives one spot in chromatography.
items.specStatementText: the concept of a pure substance
items.random_wrong: A pure substance, as it is natural

items.q: The diagram shows the particles in a sample of gas. Which statement about the sample is correct?
items.correct: It is a mixture of two elements
items.misconception: It is pure, as it has only elements
items.why: Students check whether each particle is an element and then call the whole sample an element. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) reports 13–14-year-olds who judged a mixture of two noble gases (krypton and neon) to be an element 'as "the molecules are singular"'. First count how many different kinds of particle there are. Two kinds of particle means two substances, so it is a mixture, even if both are elements.
items.specStatementText: the concept of a pure substance
items.random_wrong: It is one compound of X and Y

items.q: Rock salt is dug from the ground. Salt is extracted from it by dissolving, filtering and evaporating. Which is purer, and why?
items.correct: The extracted salt, as the rock and soil are removed
items.misconception: The rock salt, as extracting is a chemical change
items.why: The separated parts can look very different from the starting mixture. Applying this belief to chromatography spots is our inference from the finding that follows. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on introducing chemical reactions, reports Johnson (1996): children think extracted salt is 'impure' 'because it has gone through a chemical process'. Mixing and separating are physical changes. The substances that come out of a separation were in the mixture all along.
items.specStatementText: the concept of a pure substance
items.random_wrong: The rock salt, as it is natural and untouched

items.q: Sugar is added to water and dissolves. This makes a sugar solution. Which is the solute?
items.correct: The sugar that dissolves
items.misconception: The water it dissolves in
items.why: Solute and solvent are new words that look and sound alike and are learned at the same time, so students swap them. It is a common error teachers see. Solute = the substance that dissolves; solvent = the liquid it dissolves in; solution = the mixture made. Salt (solute) + water (solvent) → salty water (solution).
items.random_wrong: The sugar solution as a whole

items.q: Sugar is stirred into hot tea until it can no longer be seen. What has happened to the sugar?
items.correct: Its particles have spread out in the water
items.misconception: It has melted and become liquid sugar
items.why: Both words describe a solid seeming to turn into a liquid, and everyday speech mixes them ('the sugar melted in my tea'). Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on changes of state, summarising research: 'Melting and dissolving are used frequently as synonyms.' Melting needs only one substance and heat: the solid becomes its own liquid. Dissolving needs two substances: the particles of the solute spread out among the particles of the solvent.
items.random_wrong: It has gone and is no longer in the tea

items.q: Salt is stirred into water until no more will dissolve. More salt is then added, at the same temperature. What happens to the extra salt?
items.correct: It stays solid in the saturated solution
items.misconception: It stays solid, as salt is insoluble
items.why: Students learn 'insoluble = does not dissolve' and apply it to any solid they can see at the bottom of the liquid, without thinking about how much has already dissolved. It is a common error teachers see. Ask how much has already dissolved. Salt is soluble, but only a limited amount dissolves in a given amount of water; once that limit is reached, the solution is saturated and extra salt stays as a solid.
items.random_wrong: It dissolves if you stir for longer

items.q: Chalk powder is stirred into water. The water turns cloudy, and later the chalk settles at the bottom. What does this show?
items.correct: Chalk does not dissolve in water
items.misconception: Chalk has dissolved to make a solution
items.why: In everyday speech 'dissolved' is used loosely for anything mixed into a liquid, and the solid seems to vanish into the cloudiness. It is a common error teachers see. Check two things: is the liquid see-through, and does anything settle out when it is left to stand? A solution is see-through and nothing settles; cloudy water with bits that settle contains an insoluble solid.
items.random_wrong: Chalk dissolves with more stirring

items.q: The table shows how much of solid X dissolves in 100 g of water. A saturated solution of X in 100 g of water cools from 60 °C to 20 °C. What mass of X comes out as crystals?
items.why:
Students know that cooling makes crystals form and assume the whole solute crystallises, forgetting that the cooler water can still hold some. It is a common error teachers see. Subtract: mass that comes out = mass dissolved at the higher temperature − mass that can stay dissolved at the lower temperature.

Working: At 60 °C the saturated solution holds 50 g of X in 100 g of water. At 20 °C, 100 g of water can hold only 20 g. Mass that comes out = 50 g − 20 g = 30 g.
items.working: At 60 °C the saturated solution holds 50 g of X in 100 g of water. At 20 °C, 100 g of water can hold only 20 g. Mass that comes out = 50 g − 20 g = 30 g.

items.q: Salt is dissolved in water in a sealed flask. How does the mass of the solution compare with the mass of the salt and water before?
items.correct: The same, as the salt is still there
items.misconception: Less, as the salt has disappeared
items.why: What cannot be seen seems not to exist, and everyday speech says sugar 'disappears' in tea. The RSC Education resource 'Chemical misconceptions II: Mass and dissolving' (from Taber, 2002) notes that 'Younger students may be satisfied with the idea that solutes "disappear" when they dissolve'; Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on changes of state, reports young children saying evaporated water has 'disappeared'. Particles are far too small to see, so a substance can be present without being visible. Dissolved solids and evaporated water are still there; their particles have just spread out.
items.random_wrong: Less, as dissolved salt weighs nothing

items.q: In the particle model, what causes diffusion?
items.correct: Particles moving about at random
items.misconception: Particles that want to spread out
items.why: Everyday explanations give things feelings ('the smell wants to escape'). The University of York and Salters' Institute Best Evidence Science Teaching (BEST) teacher notes on diffusion (key concept BCL1.4) list, from research, the belief that 'molecules in an area of high concentration want to spread out, or move to seek out an area with more room'. Explain diffusion with random movement only: particles move about in all directions all the time, and the mixing happens without any purpose.
items.specStatementText: diffusion in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: A push from wind or stirring

items.q: In the particle model, why is diffusion faster at a higher temperature?
items.correct: The particles move about faster
items.misconception: The particles all get a bit bigger
items.why: Students explain what they see (things get bigger when heated) by giving the same property to the particles. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) writes: 'The idea that "materials expand on heating because the particles expand" is regarded as a common misconception.' Particles do not change size when heated. They move faster, so they spread out and mix more quickly.
items.specStatementText: diffusion in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: The heat pushes the particles along

items.q: The diagram shows gas X diffusing through gas Y in a closed box. Which statement about the X particles is correct?
items.correct: Each moves at random, but overall more go right
items.misconception: Every X particle moves only to the right
items.why: Textbooks state the rule 'from high to low concentration' and draw a single arrow, so students picture each particle following it. The BEST teacher notes on diffusion (University of York and Salters' Institute, key concept BCL1.4) list, from research, the belief that 'molecules move only in one direction, from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration'. The rule describes the overall result, not each particle. Each particle moves at random; the net movement is from higher to lower concentration.
items.specStatementText: diffusion in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: They move right because they want more room

items.q: A drop of ink is put into a beaker of still water. A day later, the colour is even all through the water. What are the ink particles doing now?
items.correct: They are still moving in all directions
items.misconception: They have stopped, as they are spread out
items.why: Nothing seems to change once the colour or smell is even, so students think nothing is moving. The BEST teacher notes on diffusion (University of York and Salters' Institute, key concept BCL1.4) list, from research, the belief that 'movement of particles stops after the concentration gradient between two areas has been equalised'. In liquids and gases, particles never stop moving. An even mixture is one where particles are still moving, but equal numbers move each way.
items.specStatementText: diffusion in terms of the particle model
items.random_wrong: They have joined water in a new compound

items.q: You want to get back both the water and the salt from salty water. Which method should you use?
items.correct: Separate it by distillation
items.misconception: Separate it by evaporation
items.why: Distillation includes an evaporation step, so students merge the two methods. It is a common error teachers see. Evaporation keeps the solid and loses the liquid. Distillation keeps both, because the condenser turns the vapour back into liquid.
items.specStatementText: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
items.random_wrong: Separate it by filtration

items.q: Salty water is poured through filter paper in a funnel. What comes through the paper?
items.correct: Water, with the salt dissolved in it
items.misconception: Only water, as the paper traps the salt
items.why: Students see filtration clean up muddy water and expect it to remove anything mixed into water; the site's own mini-lesson warns about it ('you can't filter salt out of salty water'). It is a common error teachers see. Ask whether the solid has dissolved. Undissolved bits are trapped by filter paper; dissolved particles pass through. To get dissolved salt back, use evaporation or distillation.
items.specStatementText: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
items.random_wrong: Water, with the salt melted in it

items.q: The diagram shows a paper chromatogram of a black ink. What does it show about the ink?
items.correct: It is a mixture of more than one dye
items.misconception: The top spot has the smallest particles
items.why: Filtration is usually taught first and is easy to picture, so students use the sieve idea for every method. It is a common error teachers see. Match each method to the property it uses: filtration, whether a solid has dissolved; evaporation and distillation, boiling point; chromatography, how far each dissolved substance is carried by the solvent.
items.specStatementText: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
items.random_wrong: It is one dye that has split into new dyes

items.q: A mixture contains sand, salt and water. Which plan gives dry salt with no sand in it?
items.correct: Filter, then evaporate the liquid that comes through
items.misconception: Evaporate first, then filter the dry solid that is left
items.why: Students learn each method on its own and do not think about what state the mixture is in at each step. It is a common error teachers see. Plan with the mixture in mind: use a method only when it suits what is in the mixture at that moment. Filtering works only while the salt is dissolved.
items.specStatementText: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography
items.random_wrong: Filter, then scrape the salt off the filter paper

items.q: How does a pure solid melt?
items.correct: At exactly one temperature
items.misconception: Over a range of temperatures
items.why: Students remember that 'one' and 'a range' are involved but attach them to the wrong kind of sample. It is a common error teachers see. Pure means one substance, so one temperature and one spot. A mixture has several substances, so a range of temperatures and possibly several spots.
items.random_wrong: At 0 °C, just as ice does

items.q: The graph shows the temperature of two solids, P and Q, as each is heated and melts. Which statement is correct?
items.correct: P melts at one fixed temperature, so P is pure
items.misconception: Both are solids, so both are pure substances
items.why: In everyday speech 'substance' means any kind of stuff. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) writes that to a chemist 'a substance has a definite chemical composition. To the learner any material may be considered a substance'. In science a substance has one definite make-up. Ask what the material contains: if there is more than one substance in it, it is a mixture, whatever it is called and whatever state it is in.
items.random_wrong: Q melts over a wide range, so Q is pure

items.q: Two inks are tested by paper chromatography. Ink S gives one spot. Ink T gives three spots. Which conclusion is correct?
items.correct: S may be pure; T is a mixture
items.misconception: S is a mixture, and T may be pure
items.why: Students remember that 'one' and 'a range' are involved but attach them to the wrong kind of sample. It is a common error teachers see. Pure means one substance, so one temperature and one spot. A mixture has several substances, so a range of temperatures and possibly several spots.
items.random_wrong: Both are pure, since each is one ink

items.q: Pure water boils at 100 °C. How does salty water boil?
items.correct: Higher than 100 °C, over a range
items.misconception: Lower than 100 °C, over a range
items.why: Students learn that impurities lower a melting point and carry the same rule over to boiling. It is a common error teachers see. Learn the two effects separately: impurities usually make a solid melt lower and over a range, but salty water boils higher than pure water, and over a range.
items.random_wrong: At exactly 100 °C, like water

items.q: Is a compound such as water a pure substance, even though it contains two elements?
items.correct: Yes. A pure substance can be one element or one compound. Pure water contains only H₂O molecules, so it is one substance, even though each molecule contains hydrogen and oxygen atoms.
items.misconception: Only elements can be pure: anything that contains more than one element (including a compound) is a mixture.
items.why: Students count the kinds of atom rather than the kinds of substance. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) reports 13–14-year-olds who classified a compound (CBr₄) as a mixture 'because "there are two types of element"'. Count the kinds of particle (substance), not the kinds of atom. If every particle is the same, the sample is one pure substance, whether those particles are atoms of one element or molecules of a compound.
items.specStatementText: the concept of a pure substance
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is a sample that contains atoms of two elements always a compound?
items.correct: No. It is a compound only if the atoms of the two elements are chemically joined to each other in every particle. If the two elements are just mixed, it is a mixture.
items.misconception: Any sample that contains atoms of two different elements is a compound, whether or not the atoms are joined.
items.why: Students learn that a compound contains two or more elements and apply it to the whole sample. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) reports 13–14-year-olds who judged the same mixture of krypton and neon to be a compound 'as there were "two types of atom"'. Look inside each particle. A compound's particles each contain different atoms joined together; in a mixture of elements, each particle contains only one kind of atom.
items.specStatementText: the concept of a pure substance
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is dissolving salt or sugar in water a chemical reaction that makes a new compound?
items.correct: No. A solution is a mixture. The solute is still there and can be got back unchanged, for example by evaporating the water. No new substance is made.
items.misconception: Dissolving is a chemical reaction: the solute joins with the water to make a new compound, so a solution is a compound.
items.why: The solid seems to vanish and the liquid changes (it tastes sweet or turns blue), which looks like the signs of a reaction. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on introducing chemical reactions, reports Schollum (1981): '48% of 14 year olds and 55% of 16 year olds thought sugar dissolving was a chemical change.' A solution is a mixture of solute and solvent. The particles are only spread out among each other, not joined, and the solute can be separated again by a physical method.

items.q: If you stir a saturated solution for longer, will more solid dissolve?
items.correct: No. Stirring makes a solid dissolve faster, but it does not change how much can dissolve. Once the solution is saturated, no more will dissolve at that temperature, however long you stir.
items.misconception: Stirring for longer (or harder) always makes more solid dissolve; there is no limit to how much will dissolve if you keep stirring.
items.why: In everyday life, stirring helps sugar disappear in a drink, so students link stirring with how much dissolves, not just how fast. It is a common error teachers see. Separate 'how fast' from 'how much'. Stirring and heating speed up dissolving; only a change of temperature (or more solvent) changes how much can dissolve.

items.q: To find how much solid comes out when a saturated solution cools, do you add the two solubility values?
items.correct: No. You subtract: the solid that comes out is the difference between how much was dissolved and how much can stay dissolved.
items.misconception: To find the mass of solid that comes out of solution on cooling, add the solubility values at the two temperatures.
items.why: Students pick out the two numbers in the table and combine them without asking what each one means. It is a common error teachers see. Write down what each number means before calculating: one is how much was dissolved, the other how much can stay dissolved. The difference is what comes out.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Is the solubility at the lower temperature the mass of solid that comes out on cooling?
items.correct: No. The solubility at the lower temperature is the mass that stays dissolved. The mass that comes out is how much was dissolved minus that value.
items.misconception: The mass of solid that comes out when a saturated solution is cooled is the solubility value read at the lower temperature.
items.why: Students find the row for the final temperature and give its value as the answer, without asking whether it is the mass that stays dissolved or the mass that comes out. It is a common error teachers see. The value in the table is how much can stay dissolved at that temperature. Subtract it from how much was dissolved to find how much comes out.

items.q: Does diffusion need something such as wind, currents, stirring or heat to push the particles along?
items.correct: No. Diffusion happens in perfectly still air or water. The particles' own random movement mixes them; nothing has to push them.
items.misconception: Diffusion needs an outside push, such as wind, air currents, stirring or heat pushing the particles along.
items.why: In everyday life smells are carried by draughts and drinks are mixed by stirring, so students think mixing always needs a push. The BEST teacher notes on diffusion (University of York and Salters' Institute, key concept BCL1.4) list, from research, the belief that 'diffusion requires an external force or mechanical event'. Diffusion is caused by the particles' own movement. Stirring and draughts speed up mixing, but diffusion happens without them.

items.q: When a dye diffuses through water, do the dye particles react with the water particles?
items.correct: No. Diffusion is a physical process. The particles only move among each other; no new substance is made.
items.misconception: Diffusion happens because the particles react or join with each other.
items.why: Mixing often comes with a change of colour, so students think a reaction is involved. The BEST teacher notes on diffusion (University of York and Salters' Institute, key concept BCL1.4) list, from research, the belief that 'diffusion of a substance through a solvent requires a chemical reaction'. In diffusion the particles stay the same particles. They spread out among each other without joining.

items.q: Can chromatography separate any mixture, such as salt from water?
items.correct: No. Paper chromatography separates dissolved substances that travel different distances up the paper, such as dyes. It is not a way to get a solid back from its solvent in a useful amount.
items.misconception: Chromatography can separate any mixture, including getting a dissolved solid or a liquid back from a solution.
items.why: Chromatography is taught as a separation method alongside the others, so students think it can do the same jobs. It is a common error teachers see. Use chromatography to find out which dyes (or other dissolved substances) are in a mixture. Use filtration, evaporation or distillation to get substances back.
items.specStatementText: simple techniques for separating mixtures: filtration, evaporation, distillation and chromatography

items.q: When salty water is boiled, does the salt boil off with the water?
items.correct: No. The water boils off at around 100 °C, but salt has a far higher boiling point, so the salt stays in the flask and only water vapour leaves.
items.misconception: When a solution is boiled or evaporated, the dissolved solid goes off with the solvent, so it ends up in the distillate or in the air.
items.why: Students know the solute is spread among the water particles and picture it being carried away with them. It is a common error teachers see. Each substance boils at its own temperature. At about 100 °C only the water boils away; the dissolved salt is left behind.

items.q: Does every pure substance melt at 0 °C and boil at 100 °C, like water?
items.correct: No. 0 °C and 100 °C are the melting and boiling points of pure water. Other pure substances have their own melting and boiling points.
items.misconception: All pure substances melt at 0 °C and boil at 100 °C, as water does, so a substance with other values is not pure.
items.why: Water is the main example used for melting and boiling. That students then give water's values to every pure substance is our inference from the finding that follows. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), summarising research on changes of state, notes that students 'cannot apply the same reasoning to other substances' and that 'they have learned only about the state changes of water'. Purity is shown by a sharp (fixed) melting or boiling point, not by any particular value. Each pure substance has its own values.
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Does melting always happen at a high temperature?
items.correct: No. Each substance melts at its own temperature: ice melts at 0 °C and some substances melt far below that, while others need a very high temperature.
items.misconception: Melting always needs a high (hot) temperature, and freezing always needs a low (cold) temperature.
items.why: We usually melt things by heating them and freeze things in a freezer. Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on changes of state, writes that 'The idea that freezing must occur at "cold" temperatures seems to be firmly fixed in many students'; Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 1) notes that students often expect 'all melting temperatures (even for the same substances) to always be experienced as hot'. A melting point is just a temperature, and it can be low or high. Freezing and melting of one substance happen at the same temperature.

items.q: Is the solute the same thing as the solution?
items.correct: No. The solute is only the substance that dissolves (such as sugar). The solution is the whole mixture made when it dissolves in the solvent (sugar and water together).
items.misconception: The solute is the solution: the whole mixture made by dissolving (for example, the sugar solution) is the solute.
items.why: 'Solute' and 'solution' sound alike, so students mix up the part that dissolves with the whole mixture. It is a common error teachers see. The solute is one part of the solution. Solution = solute + solvent, so the sugar solution contains the solute (sugar) and the solvent (water).
items.note: an MCQ carries this misconception as a secondary distractor only (one item per stem); its own authored question is used here; none invented

items.q: Once salt has dissolved, is it still there but weightless?
items.correct: No. The salt is still there and every salt particle keeps its mass, so the solution weighs as much as the salt and water did together.
items.misconception: A dissolved substance is still there but weighs nothing (or less), because it is floating or held up in the water.
items.why: Dissolved substances spread through the water and seem to be held up by it, like a floating object. Taber (2002, Chemical Misconceptions, RSC, vol. 1, ch. 6) reports, from a probe used with 11–13-year-olds, that 'some students are assuming that the dissolved solute has buoyancy and will not register any weight'. Every particle has mass wherever it is. Dissolved salt particles are still in the flask, so their mass still counts.

items.q: Does salty water weigh more than the salt and water did, because it is denser?
items.correct: No. Salty water is denser than pure water, but its mass is just the mass of the salt plus the mass of the water. Density is how much mass is packed into each cm³, not the total mass.
items.misconception: Heavier means denser: a liquid that becomes denser when something dissolves in it gains extra mass.
items.why: In everyday speech 'heavy' is used for both mass and density ('lead is heavier than wood'). Kind (2004, Beyond Appearances, RSC), chapter on changes of state, reports that 9–15-year-olds explain evaporation by a change in weight and that 'Stavy suggests that confusion arises because of teaching about density and weight'. Applying the same confusion to dissolving is our inference. Keep mass and density apart. Dissolving can change the density of the liquid, but the total mass is always the mass of the solute plus the mass of the solvent.
